title: Linear Search
description: Understand how linear search checks data sequentially, handles found and not-found cases, and why its runtime grows with input size.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Linear Search is the simplest searching algorithm. It works by checking elements one by one until the target is found or the collection ends.

The algorithm does not require sorting, recursion, pointer tricks, or extra data structures. It uses a direct sequential scan, which makes it one of the best first examples for understanding how search algorithms operate.

sections.title: Why Linear Search Matters
sections.content:
Many real-world systems still use sequential searching. A program may scan attendance lists, search unsorted files, check notifications, locate names in small datasets, or find a first matching record.

Linear Search matters because not all data is sorted. When the input has no useful ordering, the program may have no safe way to skip elements. It must inspect candidates directly.
bullets: It is simple to implement and debug.
It is practical for small datasets or one-time searches.

sections.title: Core Idea of Linear Search
sections.content:
Linear Search compares each array element with the target value. If the current element matches the target, the algorithm returns the current index. If the algorithm reaches the end without finding a match, it returns a not-found value such as -1.

Unlike Binary Search, Linear Search does not divide the search space or eliminate large sections. It simply checks elements in sequence.

sections.title: Searching Through an Array
sections.content:
Suppose the program searches for 11 inside the array [3, 8, 5, 11, 2]. The algorithm compares 3 with 11, then 8 with 11, then 5 with 11. None of those values match.

When the algorithm compares 11 with 11, the target is found and the index is returned. Because the target appears before the end, the algorithm can stop early.

If the program searches for a value that does not exist, every element must be checked. The algorithm reaches the end and returns -1 to communicate that the target was not found.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: A correct Linear Search implementation must include three important behaviors: sequential traversal, immediate return when a match is found, and a clear result when no match exists.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Linear Search has O(n) worst-case time complexity because the algorithm may need to inspect every element.

The best case is O(1), which happens when the target is the first element. The average and worst cases are O(n), especially when the target appears near the end or does not exist at all. Space complexity is O(1) because the algorithm only uses a small fixed amount of extra memory.

chart.title: Linear Search growth
chart.description: Linear Search grows proportionally with input size. The chart compares O(1), O(n), and O(log n) so the sequential scan can be contrasted with constant and logarithmic behavior.

subsections.title: Best Case
subsections.content: The best case occurs when the target appears immediately. For example, searching for 8 inside [8, 3, 5, 1] requires only one comparison.

subsections.title: Worst Case
subsections.content: The worst case occurs when the target is at the end or missing. Searching for 10 inside [3, 8, 5, 11, 2] checks every element before returning -1.

sections.title: Linear Search vs Binary Search
sections.content:
Linear Search works on unsorted data and scans sequentially. Binary Search requires sorted data and uses a divide-and-conquer strategy to eliminate half of the remaining search space after each comparison.

This means Linear Search is simpler and more flexible, while Binary Search is much more scalable when the data is already sorted.

subsections.title: Advantages
bullets: The algorithm uses O(1) auxiliary space.
It is effective for small datasets and simple checks.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: Large datasets can require many comparisons.
Repeated searches over huge arrays become expensive.
It does not use ordering or indexing to skip work.
Optimized search algorithms are better when data is structured.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Linear Search appears in simple mobile apps, validation systems, small configuration lists, file scanning tools, and situations where data arrives unsorted.

It is also commonly used as a teaching algorithm because it clearly shows comparison flow, stopping conditions, and the relationship between input size and runtime.

subsections.title: Mistake: Forgetting to stop after a match
subsections.content: When the task asks for the first matching index, the algorithm should return immediately after the first match is found.

subsections.title: Mistake: Returning the element instead of the index
subsections.content: Many search tasks ask for the position of the target, not the target value itself. The return value must match the requirement.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring the not-found case
subsections.content: A search algorithm must define what happens when the target does not exist. In many beginner problems, -1 is used for this case.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The best case is O(1) when the first item matches.
The worst case is O(n) when the target is missing or near the end.
Linear Search is simple and reliable, but not ideal for repeated searches over large datasets.
